sections.h2: How is North Dakota organized, and who handles a house sale?
sections.html:
North Dakota has 53 counties, and the county is the level of government that touches most of a home sale. Property tax bills, recorded deeds and probate filings all run through county offices, so a seller in Fargo and a seller in Williston deal with different courthouses even though the state rules are the same.

The seven counties below hold the cities we cover most often. County seats and population figures come from Wikipedia's county list, which draws on Census data.

  • Cass County (seat: Fargo), about 201,800 residents
  • Burleigh County (seat: Bismarck), about 103,300
  • Grand Forks County (seat: Grand Forks), about 74,500
  • Ward County (seat: Minot), about 68,200
  • Williams County (seat: Williston), about 41,800
  • Morton County (seat: Mandan), about 34,600
  • Stark County (seat: Dickinson), about 34,000

West Fargo is not a county seat. It sits in Cass County, next to Fargo.

sections.h2: When are North Dakota property taxes due, and what happens if a sale closes mid-year?
sections.html:
Real estate tax is due on January 1 for the prior year's levy, and the State Tax Commissioner's calendar sets the payment dates that follow.

  • February 1: assessment date for real property.
  • February 15: last day to pay the full year and take the 5 percent discount.
  • March 1: last day to pay the first installment without penalty. Penalties start the next day and step up on May 1, July 1 and October 15.
  • October 15: last day to pay the second installment without penalty.
  • December 26: the county treasurer mails the new property tax statements.

The same calendar says township and city boards of equalization meet in April, the county board meets in the first 10 days of June, and the State Board meets on the second Tuesday in August to review local assessments. If you think your value is too high, the June county meeting is where most owners start.

Unpaid tax does not block a sale. It is usually paid out of the seller's proceeds at closing, and the title company asks the treasurer for a payoff figure. Our North Dakota property tax guide walks through appeals, exemptions and selling with tax due. City readers can also use the Fargo, Bismarck and Grand Forks tax guides.

sections.h2: Does North Dakota charge a deed or transfer tax?
sections.html:
No. The Grand Forks County Recorder's page states that North Dakota does not have a deed or mortgage tax. That removes one cost that sellers in many other states have to budget for.

Recording still happens at the county recorder, who keeps the permanent record of documents that affect title to real property. Recorders charge fees for copies and filings. Grand Forks County lists $1.00 per page for a copy and $5.00 for the first page of a certified copy. Other counties set their own schedules, so ask the recorder where your house sits.

sections.h2: How does foreclosure work in North Dakota?
sections.html:
Foreclosure in North Dakota is judicial, which means the lender has to sue and get a court order before a house can be sold. For an owner who is behind on payments, that adds a few steps and some time.

  1. The lender serves a notice at least 30 days, and no more than 90 days, before it files the lawsuit. The notice gives the borrower 30 days to bring the loan current.
  2. If the borrower does not cure, the lender files a complaint and summons in court.
  3. After judgment, an officer sells the property at auction. Notice of the sale is published in a newspaper once a week for three weeks.
  4. After the sale, the borrower generally has 60 days to redeem. Abandoned property and agricultural land follow different rules.

Deficiency judgments are barred for owner-occupied residential property of four or fewer units on up to 40 contiguous acres. If a third party bids more than the debt, the extra money belongs to the owner, though a small surplus under $1,000 can be forfeited to the county if nobody claims it within 60 days. These points come from Nolo's summary of chapter 32-19 of the North Dakota Century Code. Read the statute or talk to a North Dakota attorney before you rely on a deadline.

sections.h2: What happens to an inherited house in North Dakota?
sections.html:
North Dakota has adopted the Uniform Probate Code. The North Dakota Court System says that lets many estates open informally, without a hearing, when the right forms are filed. A personal representative has to be appointed before anyone can sell the house on behalf of the estate, and probate is the only way to get one appointed.

  • Informal probate is generally available when less than 3 years have passed since the date of death.
  • The validity of the will cannot be disputed.
  • Everyone with equal or higher priority has to agree on who serves as personal representative.

If a will is contested, or the family cannot agree, the estate moves to formal probate, which takes longer. Informal probate also works when there is no will. The Court System publishes a free guidebook and forms, and suggests a lawyer if the paperwork is unclear.

sections.h2: What is the North Dakota homestead exemption, and does it affect a sale?
sections.html:
The homestead exemption protects up to $150,000 of home equity from creditors in bankruptcy. Nolo reports the figure last changed on July 1, 2023, and that spouses filing jointly do not double it. To claim it, the owner must live in North Dakota and live on the property.

If you are weighing bankruptcy and a sale together, talk to a bankruptcy attorney first, because the order of events matters.

sections.h2: What if the house has tenants?
sections.html:
Tenants do not stop you from selling, but the deposit has to follow the house. Under chapter 47-16 of the Century Code, when a rental changes hands the security deposit and accrued interest must be transferred to the new owner, and the seller stays liable until that happens. A landlord may also enter to show the unit to a buyer, after giving notice and seeking the tenant's consent to a set time.

Our landlord and tenant guide covers deposits, entry and notice rules in more detail. If someone is living in a house without a lease or permission, see squatters rights and adverse possession.

sections.h2: Does flood risk change how a North Dakota house sells?
sections.html:
It can, especially along the Red River. Fargo's Red River minor flood stage starts at 18 feet and major flooding begins at 30 feet. The river crested at a record 39.5 feet in 1997 and at 40.84 feet in 2009, according to Wikipedia's Fargo article. The city has bought hundreds of houses in flood-prone areas, and a large diversion project is under construction.

A buyer will ask where the house sits relative to the floodplain and whether it has flood insurance. Pull the flood map for the parcel and gather any claim history before you list or take offers. Radon, well and septic conditions also vary by property, so ask your county or local public health unit.

sections.h2: What does a cash, as-is sale mean in North Dakota?
sections.html:
It means the buyer pays without a mortgage and takes the house in its current condition, so there is no lender appraisal and no repair list to negotiate. The seller still signs a deed, and a title company or attorney still searches title and handles the closing. Which of those you use is your choice, and costs are set by the provider, so ask each one for a written estimate.

Cash is most useful when the house has a problem that stalls a regular listing: a probate that needs to close, a foreclosure clock, a tenant, or repairs you cannot fund. Our city pages explain how this works locally for Fargo, Bismarck, Grand Forks and the other cities listed below. For tax, probate and foreclosure by county, start with our North Dakota guides by city and county.

faqs.q: How many counties does North Dakota have?
faqs.a: North Dakota has 53 counties. Most seller paperwork, including tax bills and recorded deeds, is handled by the county where the house sits.

faqs.q: Does North Dakota have a transfer tax on deeds?
faqs.a: No. The Grand Forks County Recorder states that North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax. Recording fees still apply, and each county sets its own.

faqs.q: Is foreclosure in North Dakota judicial?
faqs.a: Yes. The lender must file a lawsuit and win a court order before a sale. Generally the owner can redeem within 60 days after the sale, with exceptions for abandoned and agricultural property.

faqs.q: When are North Dakota property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first installment is due March 1 and the second October 15. Paying the full year by February 15 earns a 5 percent discount.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited house before probate is finished?
faqs.a: A personal representative must be appointed first. Informal probate, often available within 3 years of death, can do that without a hearing.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house with tenants in North Dakota?
faqs.a: Yes. The security deposit and interest must be transferred to the new owner, and the seller stays liable until it is.

faqs.q: Will a cash buyer pay for repairs?
faqs.a: A cash as-is buyer takes the house in its current condition, so you do not need to fix it first. Ask for the terms in writing.
